summary: This experimental RFC extends SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND), which protects IPv6 neighbor discovery with digital signatures. Plain SEND assumes the sender holds the keys for the address it speaks for, so a proxy that answers on another node's behalf cannot use it. The document defines how proxies can take part in SEND securely, mainly for mobility scenarios.

plainLanguage.summary: Imagine a letter that must be signed by its owner. But sometimes a helper has to answer for someone who is away. This is a way to let the helper sign safely, so nobody can pretend to be the helper.

questions: how does send work with a proxy
secure neighbor discovery for mobile ipv6
subtitle: Digital signatures for IPv6 proxies answering on behalf of other nodes.

tldr.problem: SEcure Neighbor Discovery (SEND) requires nodes to sign their own ND messages with their private keys, but proxies that answer on behalf of other nodes cannot do this since they lack the owner's private key.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC extends SEND by introducing a Proxy Signature option that lets authorized proxies sign messages with their own keys instead, proven valid through a certificate that explicitly authorizes the proxy to speak for certain addresses.
tldr.outcome: Proxies can now securely participate in SEND-protected networks. This is crucial for mobility scenarios like Mobile IPv6 and Proxy Mobile IPv6, where a home agent or access gateway must answer ND queries without possessing the mobile node's keys.

today: RFC 6496 remains Experimental. It defined the mechanism for securing ND proxy operations but has not been moved to Standards Track. The specification is used in some mobility deployments and remains relevant for environments where SEND protection and proxying must coexist, though adoption has been limited.

sections.title: Why Proxies Need Signatures
sections.content:
SEND protects IPv6 neighbor discovery by requiring nodes to sign each message with their own private key, proving ownership of an address. However, proxies—nodes that answer ND queries on behalf of other nodes—do not have the private keys of the nodes they represent. This creates a conflict: the original SEND specification provides no way for a proxy to securely answer on another node's behalf.

This document solves the problem by introducing a way for trusted proxies to sign messages using their own keys, with explicit certificates that prove they are authorized to proxy for specific addresses.
sections.plainLanguage: A proxy is like a secretary: it has to answer for the boss when the boss is busy. The secretary needs to prove it is allowed to speak for the boss.

sections.title: The Proxy Signature Option
sections.content:
The RFC introduces a new Proxy Signature (PS) option for ND messages. The PS option contains a digital signature generated by the proxy's private key, along with a 128-bit hash of the proxy's public key (computed using SHA-1). When an ND message includes a PS option, it MUST NOT contain the original CGA or RSA Signature options that SEND uses for direct ownership.

The signature is computed over the IP header (source and destination addresses), the ICMP header, the NDP message header, and all ND options preceding the PS option. This ensures the entire message is signed and cannot be modified in transit.

The proxy must hold a special Secure Proxy ND certificate, an X.509v3 certificate that explicitly authorizes the proxy to sign messages for specific address prefixes. The certificate includes KeyPurposeId extensions that specify which types of messages the proxy can sign (such as Router Advertisements or Neighbor Advertisements).
sections.plainLanguage: The proxy writes its signature and proof of who it is inside the message. The signature covers everything so nobody can change it.

sections.title: How Proxies Sign Messages
sections.content:
When a Secure ND Proxy generates or translates an ND message on behalf of a proxied address, it follows these steps: First, it builds the ND message according to normal rules. Then it adds a Timestamp option (generated by the proxy) and, if needed, a Nonce option (taken from a received solicitation or generated by the proxy). Finally, it appends the Proxy Signature option containing the signature and the hash of its public key.

The proxy must verify that the Key Purpose Id in its certificate grants it permission to sign the type of message (Router Advertisement, Neighbor Advertisement, Router Solicitation, Neighbor Solicitation, or Redirect). For Router Advertisements and Redirects, the proxy must ensure the prefix or target address falls within the range authorized by the certificate. For other message types, the source address must fall within the authorized prefix.
sections.plainLanguage: The proxy adds a timestamp, signs the message, and puts its signature inside. Receivers check the signature and the certificate to trust the message.

sections.title: Receiving and Verifying Proxy Messages
sections.content:
Nodes that receive ND messages with Proxy Signature options (called SPND nodes) must know the proxy's certificate and verify the signature. The receiver checks that the Key Hash in the PS option matches a known public key, that a valid certification path exists from the receiver's trust anchor to the proxy's key, and that the certificate includes the appropriate KeyPurposeId and prefix for the message type.

The receiver then verifies the digital signature was computed correctly and checks Timestamp and Nonce options to prevent replay attacks. If verification succeeds, the message is considered secure. If it fails, the message is silently discarded if the node is configured to accept only secured messages, or treated as unsecured if the node accepts both types.
sections.plainLanguage: The receiver checks that it knows the proxy, that the proxy's certificate allows it to sign this type of message, and that the signature is correct.

sections.title: Real-World Applications
sections.content:
The RFC describes three main deployment scenarios. In Mobile IPv6, a Home Agent proxies ND messages while a Mobile Node is away from home, proving ownership of the node's address using a Secure Proxy ND certificate. In Proxy Mobile IPv6, Mobile Access Gateways (MAGs) proxy messages on behalf of Mobile Nodes, with all MAGs sharing a domain-level certificate to ensure consistent link-layer addresses. In RFC 4389 ND Proxy, an ND proxy bridges multiple link-layer segments and securely proxies ND messages between them, validating incoming messages and signing outgoing ones.

In all cases, the proxy's certificate explicitly authorizes it to proxy for specific prefixes, and receivers can verify that proxied messages are legitimate by checking the certificate and signature.
sections.plainLanguage: Home agents protect addresses while people travel. Gateways protect addresses when people move between networks. Bridges protect addresses between different physical links.

sections.title: Working With Older Nodes
sections.content:
The RFC ensures backward compatibility. Old SEND nodes (RFC 3971) that do not implement Secure Proxy ND support will silently discard the PS option, treating proxied messages as unsecured. Non-SEND nodes also silently discard PS options as unknown ND options. This allows a mixed network of old and new nodes to coexist.

However, a Secure ND Proxy must be careful when proxying for nodes that may return to the same link. If a Mobile Node can return home, the proxy should only sign messages on behalf of nodes with SEND capability (RFC 3971 or SPND nodes), to avoid giving proxied messages undue preference over messages from the node itself.
sections.plainLanguage: Old devices do not understand the proxy signature, so they ignore it. New devices understand and check it. Both can live together in the same network.
